559366227.name: Renaissance and Enlightenment: religion and thought
559366227.outcome: I can explain how changes in worldviews during the Renaissance and the Enlightenment period impacted religion's role in society, including in political life.
points: Some worldviews are collective, reflecting the shared values of a society or era.
The Renaissance marks the end of the Middle Ages & is characterised by striving for progress in thought and creativity.
The Age of Enlightenment was an intellectual and philosophical movement in 17th and 18th-century Europe.
As the worldview of the Middle Ages changed, the Church’s control over politics and life lessened.
keywords: a 17th and 18th-century movement emphasising reason, science and individual rights
a movement that emphasised the value of human potential, drawing inspiration from classical Greek and Roman ideas
the activities and decisions involved in governing a society or state
a period of cultural, artistic, scientific and intellectual rebirth in Europe from the 14th to the 17th century
tips: Look at the Year 7 unit 'Exploring philosophy' for some background to the ideas and methods rediscovered during the Enlightenment.

56978638.name: The philosophy and beliefs of Thomas Hobbes
56978638.outcome: I can explain who Thomas Hobbes was, his context, and why his religious views were considered controversial.
points: Thomas Hobbes was an English philosopher who lived during the Renaissance and Enlightenment period.
He is most famous for his political philosophy and his 1651 book, 'Leviathan'.
Hobbes provided a cosmological argument for the existence of God, saying that God is "the first cause of all causes".
There is debate about what Hobbes' religious views were as he held some contradicting views.
One example of this contradiction is that he denies the existence of a soul but accepts the existence of God.
keywords: an argument that attempts to prove God's existence as the first cause of the universe.
a book by Thomas Hobbes that argues for a strong authority to maintain order in society
the belief that everything, including thoughts and emotions, arises from physical matter
an English philosopher (1588–1679) known for his political philosophy
tips: Task B2 could be used as part of a larger piece of work on how Hobbes and Rousseau aligned religion and politics. It could be completed as an oracy task or as a cloze (fill in the gaps) exercise.

389593490.name: The state of nature and social contracts
389593490.outcome: I can explain Thomas Hobbes’ ideas about the state of nature, the social contract and the role of a sovereign.
points: Hobbes explains the state of nature and the social contract in his work 'Leviathan'.
The state of nature according to Hobbes is everybody living for themselves.
He believed that when people have unlimited freedom, it leads to chaos and a war-like scenario.
Hobbes argues that social contracts limit our freedom but provide benefits such as security.
Social contracts need to be enacted by a sovereign or ruler and work to bring the state of nature to an end.
keywords: the power to give orders, make decisions and enforce obedience
the natural liberty to act as one wishes
a concept that imagines life without society or government, with different philosophers seeing it as either peaceful or chaotic
a philosophical tool to test ideas in hypothetical contexts, not real-world scenarios
tips: Organise a class debate about the state of nature, with students presenting both Hobbes' view and arguments against it.

23926186.name: The philosophy and beliefs of Jean-Jacques Rousseau
23926186.outcome: I can explain Rousseau's ideas about human nature and society and link them to his religious views.
points: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was an Enlightenment philosopher.
Many believed his views to be radical.
Rousseau's core belief was that humans are mostly good and it is society that corrupts them.
He argued that humans were more civilised in their natural state than in civilisations.
Rousseau believed in God and the afterlife but was Protestant and Catholic at different points in his life.
keywords: a society with organised communities, rules, and developed ways of living
Rousseau's idea of a set of shared beliefs that unite people, without specific religious practices
a Swiss philosopher (1712–1778) known for his political philosophy
a teaching style attributed to Socrates which involves asking questions
tips: Check students have an understanding of the reformation and the difference between Protestantism and Catholicism.

740775474.name: Analysing 'The Social Contract' by Rousseau
740775474.outcome: I can analyse Rousseau's idea of the social contract and how it relates to freedom and the general will.
points: Rousseau's main work was called 'The Social Contract.
This sets out his beliefs about human goodness and how society should be run.
He argues that people are free when governed by their own laws, serving the interest of the greater good.
Rousseau believed in elected officials carrying out the will of the people.
We can use critical thinking to analyse Rousseau’s idea of a social contract.
keywords: according to Rousseau, individuals chosen by the people to implement the general will
the collective will of the people, focused on what is best for society as a whole, and not individual desires
Rousseau's 1762 book and idea that individuals must give up some freedoms to form a just society, with laws reflecting the common good
tips: Organise a debate between students on whether when we live in a society or groups, we form unwritten agreements about how to live together.

561475420.name: Interaction between religious, philosophical and political belief
561475420.outcome: I can explain how Enlightenment thinking challenged Middle Ages views, focusing on empiricism, deism and the separation of Church and state.
points: To understand religious and philosophical views from a different time period, context is very important.
Enlightenment thinking was influenced by changes in approaches to the arts and by religious reform.
Enlightenment philosophers used empiricism to challenge superstitious religious views.
This made it possible to move away from the worldview of the Middle Ages. One example of this, was deism.
The Enlightenment shifted to advocating for a separation of religion and politics.
keywords: the belief in a creator God who does not intervene in the universe after creating it
the philosophical theory that knowledge comes from sensory experience and observation
a belief based on fear or misunderstanding of the unknown, which goes beyond what is logical
tips: Make links with reasons for the Reformation in Europe.

549160494.name: William James and mystical experience
549160494.outcome: I can explain William James' understanding of religious and mystical experiences and how they contribute to the question of God's existence.
points: William James studied religious experiences from a psychologist's perspective and explained their impact on philosophy.
He relied on observation, conversation and evidence of impact to reach his conclusions.
William James identified four features of mystical experience.
He did not seek to prove the existence of a particular God or gods.
William James concluded that his research leads to a likelihood of a god existing.
keywords: a religious experience where someone feels a deep personal connection to a higher power
a philosophical approach that assesses ideas based on their usefulness in real-life situations
personal feeling or moment when someone believes they connect with a higher power
20th century psychologist and philosopher who popularised pragmatism
tips: Task C could be used as either an oracy or an extended writing task.

577031095.name: Persinger's God helmet
577031095.outcome: I can explain Persinger’s God helmet experiment and evaluate its implications for the existence of God.
points: The God helmet is an experiment designed to see if feelings of religious experience can be induced.
In the experiment, the temporal lobe is stimulated based on testimony of those with temporal lobe epilepsy.
The stimulation brought about effects similar to those of people claiming a religious experience.
Some claim this experiment proves God does not exist, or at least that religious experience is not genuine.
Others argue that a creator God designed the human brain to include the temporal lobe as a channel of communication.
keywords: facts or information that supports an idea
a device that stimulates the temporal lobes with electromagnetic fields to induce religious experiences
a neuroscientist known for developing the God helmet to study the brain's role in religious experiences
a philosophical tool that encourages questioning and doubting things to ensure we have good evidence before believing them
tips: For additional material A, encourage discussion about how points in the story could be understood differently. Task B part 2 could be used as an extended writing activity or a cloze task (using the sample answer with gaps for students). Teachers could search online for a picture of the God helmet.

827007893.name: Ian McCormack and near death experience
827007893.outcome: I can reflect on Ian McCormack’s conversion experience and use philosophical arguments to show how it could be used as support for the existence of God.
points: People may have religious experiences that confirm their current beliefs or convert them to a new religious outlook.
Ian McCormack was an atheist who had a near death experience and became a Christian.
Following his near death experience and conversion, he has dedicated his life to spreading Christianity.
Richard Swinburne argues the role of credulity and testimony support the validity of religious experiences.
Philosophers may argue that whether his experience can be proven is less significant than the impact it has had.
keywords: a complete transformation, often involving a change in worldview, such as adopting a new religious belief
a man who converted to Christianity after having a near death experience
a transformative experience often involving visions, feelings of peace or encounters with a higher power, typically reported by those who have been close to death
a philosopher who argues that religious experiences should be taken as evidence for the existence of God
tips: Teachers could show a clip of Ian McCormack sharing his testimony or parts of the film about his experience 'The Perfect Wave'. Task B could be adapted as an oracy task or cloze task using the sample answers (students are presented text with key elements missing for them to complete).

guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

210986794.name: St Bernadette of Lourdes
210986794.outcome: I can explain what St Bernadette learned through her visions and reflect on whether she had knowledge of God.
points: Bernadette experienced visions of the Virgin Mary, who asked for a chapel to be built by a nearby muddy cave.
Mary told her to drink the muddy water of the spring and the next day it flowed with clear water.
Her body is said by the Catholic Church to remain internally incorrupt and she was named a saint.
Lourdes is a place of pilgrimage for Christians, with the water said to have healing properties.
Some philosophers would argue that Bernadette gained knowledge of God although others would disagree.
keywords: understanding or information believed to be true and supported by reasons
a French town where St Bernadette’s visions of Mary occurred, now a pilgrimage site
a girl who reported visions of Mary in 1858, inspiring the Lourdes pilgrimage
the mother of Jesus, particularly honoured in Catholicism as pure and a helper in prayer
a religious experience where a person sees or feels a divine or spiritual presence
tips: Task B could be completed as an extended writing task with students writing paragraphs using their learning on St Bernadette to answer the question 'Do religious experiences prove God exists?'. It could also form the basis of an oracy task with students role-playing or debating the question.

668501947.name: Sufism and connecting with Allah
668501947.outcome: I can explain how Sufis connect with Allah and why some Muslims would say knowledge cannot be gained through Sufi mysticism.
points: Sufism may be described as Islamic mysticism
Sufis exist within Sunni and Shi'a Islam, rather than being a distinct religious group.
Sufi Muslims try to achieve direct personal experience of Allah.
Other Muslims may disagree with the idea of trying to get personal experience of God.
keywords: Arabic word for God (literally means 'the God')
used by Sufis to describe deep, personal knowledge of Allah that comes from spiritual experiences
a way of experiencing and connecting with Allah through personal, inner experiences
a mystical approach in Islam that focuses on achieving ma’rifah (true knowledge of Allah) through a deep, personal connection with him
tips: You might like to show a video of whirling. Task B2 could become an oracy task or cloze task (providing the answer with key gaps to fill).

589368189.name: Atman: the divine within all
589368189.outcome: I can explain different understandings of the atman as divine and evaluate the claim that experiences across religions cancel each other out.
points: Atman is a Sanskrit word for the true or eternal self and most Hindus believe it is in every living being.
Atman comes from Brahman and could be seen as a part of the ultimate being within each of us.
In different Indian philosophies, atman is part of the individual self and ultimate reality or completely separate.
The multiple claims issue is the problem that conflicting religious experiences challenge the proof of one specific God.
John Hick argues that religious pluralism means different religious experiences interpret the same divine reality.
keywords: the spark of Brahman or spirit within all living beings
the supreme spirit or ultimate reality
philosopher who argues for religious pluralism
conflicting religious experiences challenge the idea they can prove the existence of God
someone who believes that different religions are paths to understanding the same divine truth
tips: An introduction to atman, Brahman and reincarnation in Hindu Dharma might be a useful preliminary task.

603233530.name: Ten Commandments
603233530.outcome: I can explain the context for the Ten Commandments and their relevance today for people of different worldviews.
points: The Ten Commandments were revealed to Moses and are contained in the story of the Exodus.
The Israelites had begun to act in a way that displeased God while they wandered in the desert so God sent clear rules.
These became the basis for moral living for Jews and later, Christians.
The influence of the Ten Commandments can be seen in modern times and impact present day British law.
Some of the Commandments are not illegal in modern society, but believers may find breaking them immoral or sinful.
keywords: a divine rule, given by God
a book of the Bible which contains the 10 Commandments
messenger or prophet of the Abrahamic religions
tips: To consolidate the learning in this lesson ensure that the students know the story of Moses and the Israelites from the book of Exodus.

404592997.name: Two great Commandments
404592997.outcome: I can explain the meaning of the two great Commandments and their relevance for Christians today.
points: The two great Commandments are contained in the New Testament.
You could categorise the Ten Commandments under the two great Commandment headings.
Jesus told the parable of the Good Samaritan to help people understand what it means to 'love your neighbour'.
Christians may be guided by these Commandments when making moral decisions.
keywords: refers to an important rule given by God that tells people how to behave
in the Bible, refers to anyone in need of help or compassion
a story used to illustrate a moral lesson, as told by Jesus in the Gospels
tips: To consolidate the learning in this lesson, ensure pupils are familiar with the Good Samaritan parable.

111190631.name: Situation ethics of Jesus
111190631.outcome: I can explain what is meant by situation ethics and describe examples from the life of Jesus that might encourage Christians to take this approach.
points: Situation ethics determines what is right based on a specific situation, rather than by strict adherence to laws.
Christians can use the teachings of Jesus in the New Testament as a source of authority on how to apply the law.
Jesus emphasised doing the most loving thing in any situation, which can be called situation ethics.
Agape love is prioritised above other considerations and impacted the example of Jesus on how the law should be applied.
Examples can be found in the Bible where Jesus recommended going against the law to do the most loving thing.
keywords: a type of non-romantic love, characterised by selfless and unconditional giving
relating to beliefs about what is morally right and wrong
the system of rules which a particular country or community recognises, which it may enforce by the imposition of penalties
an ethical theory which argues that the most loving action should guide decisions in each situation
tips: You will be able to find additional parables of Jesus showing agape to give wider context, such as Luke 15:11-32.

366788495.name: Muslims and Shariah Law
366788495.outcome: I can describe what is meant by Shariah and how many Muslims explain its origins.
points: The word Shariah means path to a water source. This is interpreted by many Muslims as an attractive path to follow.
Most Muslims have two main sources of authority; the Qur'an and the Sunnah.
These two sources make up the Shariah.
The Shariah came about at a time of Muslim migration as the first Muslim communities were being established.
keywords: a set of moral and religious rules that guide Muslims
the recorded words of the Prophet Muhammad
actions or things which are permitted within Islam
any actions or things which are forbidden within Islam
refers to the migration of the Prophet Muhammad and his followers
tips: The distance from Makkah to Madinah is approximately 450 kilometers (280 miles) by road. Ask pupils to consider the challenges that the first Muslim community would have faced, making that journey by foot or camel.

397816368.name: Interpreting Shariah using ijtihad
397816368.outcome: I can explain the meaning of ijtihad and how it might be interpreted and applied by Muslims today.
points: Muslim thinking has developed since Prophet Muhammad. A challenge has been to respond to ideas not in Qur'an or Hadith.
The term ‘ijtihad’ comes from the word jihad, which means struggle, effort or fight.
Ijtihad is the method of using the principles of the Qur'an and Hadith to identify the best action.
Using ijtihad may result in different interpretations which lead to diversity of thought amongst different Muslims.
keywords: the recorded words of the Prophet Muhammad
the human effort and reasoning used to work out the Shariah
the action of explaining the meaning of something
a set of moral and religious laws that guide Muslims
tips: Connect ijtihad to real-life situations students can relate to e.g., social media, AI, climate change, or everyday moral dilemmas.

871444735.name: Using ijtihad to understand differing Muslim attitudes to music
871444735.outcome: I can analyse different Islamic sources to better understand different Muslim worldviews regarding music.
points: The topic of music is something debated in Islam as to whether it is halal or haram.
Some Muslims believe that music is haram and interpret Islamic sources to make this argument.
Other Muslims interpret the sources differently to argue certain forms of music are permissible.
Analysing the way the different sources have been interpreted can allow us to better understand Muslim worldviews.
keywords: actions or things which are permitted within Islam
any actions or things which are forbidden within Islam
the human effort and reasoning used to work out the Shariah
a set of moral and religious laws that guide Muslims
a person's way of understanding, experiencing and responding to the world
tips: Listen to a clip from Muslim musician Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan.

222598388.name: Martin Luther and the Reformation
222598388.outcome: I can explain how and why Martin Luther rebelled against the religious authorities of his time.
points: Martin Luther rebelled against the religious authority of his time.
Martin Luther was an important figure in the Protestant Reformation.
He rebelled against what he understood to be incorrect beliefs and practices in the Roman Catholic Church at his time.
The author and context of a historical source should be considered when assessing its usefulness.
keywords: ways through which Christians in the Catholic Church may be granted some reduction in the punishment of sins after forgiveness by God
a Christian religious movement in the 16th century that aimed to reform the Catholic Church, but caused new denominations to be created
the process or place where a person's soul is prepared for heaven after death
statements or ideas put forward for discussion, argument or debate
a member of a religious group of men who often live separate from the rest of society
tips: There are myths and misconceptions around indulgences and the Roman Catholic Church which teachers should take care with. These can be further explored and understood from the Catholic perspective via sites such as: https://www.catholic.com/tract/myths-about-indulgences.

748263276.name: Reaching heaven by faith alone
748263276.outcome: I can explain how Martin Luther's teaching on reaching heaven by faith alone may influence Christians today.
points: Martin Luther emphasised the idea that Christians will reach heaven through their faith in Jesus, not works.
Martin Luther emphasised that the main authority for Christians should be the Bible as a scripture.
Reaching heaven through faith alone continues to be an influential Christian idea today.
Evangelical Christianity today is influenced by Martin Luther's ideas.
Different types of data can have different uses as tools to help us know more about religions.
keywords: an interpretation of Christianity that emphasises the authority of the Bible and the need for a personal faith in Jesus Christ
faith alone, the principle that it is faith, not works, that will help someone get to heaven
actions or deeds that God has commanded or sees as good
tips: Students may like to listen to the songs "Amazing Grace" and "Blinded by your Grace", which are referenced in this lesson. The lives of John Newton and Stormzy can also be explored in relation to their Christian faith.

292039824.name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer, the pacifist
292039824.outcome: I can explain how and why Bonhoeffer rebelled against the authorities of his time.
points: Dietrich Bonhoeffer rebelled against the political authorities of his time.
Dietrich Bonhoeffer was an important figure in the resistance against the Nazi Party of Germany between 1933 and 1945.
Dietrick Bonhoeffer was a pacifist who faced moral dilemmas relating to his resistance against the Nazi Party.
Current cultural artefacts can inform us of the importance of the beliefs and actions of rebels from the past.
keywords: a difficult choice between two or more options, often involving a moral or ethical conflict
the systematic persecution and murder of European Jews and other groups by the Nazis
a person who suffers or dies for their beliefs or principles and is often seen as a hero or symbol of a cause
a person who believes in resolving conflicts without violence and opposes war or the use of force
opposition and disobedience to the Nazi regime
tips: To consider making links wtih with other activities in school around commemorating Holocaust Memorial Day (27th January)

guidance.description: Discriminatory behaviour or images, whether on the grounds of race, gender, disability, religion or belief or sexual orientation, or otherwise.

114581446.name: Fighting against unjust laws
114581446.outcome: I can explain how and why people may choose to fight against unjust laws.
points: There are a variety of reasons why societies have laws.
Social scientists look at the laws of a society to see the values and normal behaviour in that society.
Augustine argued that 'an unjust law is no law at all'.
There are examples of people who have fought against unjust laws.
Religious ideas can support following laws, as well as fighting against unjust laws.
keywords: the unfair treatment of a people and groups based on a part of their identity such as sex, race or religion
the idea that everyone should get fair reward or punishment for their actions
a rule, usually made by a government, that is used to order the way in which a society behaves
a person who believes in resolving conflicts without violence and opposes war or the use of force
when something is unfair or treats people unequally
tips: Students can listen to "If you miss me at the back of the bus" by Pete Seeger, a protest song about Rosa Parks and analyse the lyrics and/or write their own verses about other people who have fought against unjust laws.

335565590.name: Vandana Shiva: protecting the earth
335565590.outcome: I can explain how and why Vandana Shiva rebelled against the authorities of her time.
points: Vandana Shiva is an influential Hindu environmental campaigner and ecofeminist.
Vandana Shiva has rebelled against what she understands to be an economic system that is using the earth for profit.
Vandana Shiva's worldview is shaped by a passion for protecting biodiversity and Hindu understandings of the world.
Questions raised by social scientists on power structures in society can help us better understand her rebellion.
keywords: a person who works to bring about political or social changes through different means
the range of different organisms (species) that live in a place
the idea that caring for the environment and equality between men and women are connected issues
changing the genetic structure of something using bio-technology
many different parts connected to each other to form a whole
tips: Vandana Shiva speaks eloquantly about things that shaped her worldview in various interviews online - teachers and students may find it helpful to hear her speak of these things in her own words.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
guidance.description: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

320700128.name: Dharma, Bhumi and the environment
320700128.outcome: I can explain why and how the concept of dharma and the figure of Bhumi may encourage some Hindus to care for the environment.
points: The concept of Dharma and human responsibility can encourage Hindus to care for the environment.
The figure of Bhumi as sacred mother earth can encourage Hindus to care for the environment.
All living things on earth contain within them the atman as a spark of the divine.
The principle of ahimsa means that many Hindus are vegetarian, and this can also benefit the environment.
All living things should be treated with compassion according to Hindu teachings about human dharma.
keywords: the principle of non-violence towards any living thing
the earth or earth goddess, representing the natural world and all the life it sustains
the essence of things, the eternal laws that sustain the universe
something that is considered holy, divine, or deserving of great respect and reverence
someone who does not eat any meat, fish or poultry
tips: Organisations such as Bhumi Global would make another interesting case study for Hindu communities taking action to preserve and replenish the natural world and its inhabitants.

225336648.name: Interpreting the 2021 census data
225336648.outcome: I can explain how the census asks about religion and what the results can and cannot tell us about religion in England and Wales.
points: There are key differences regarding the religion data from the 2011 and 2021 census data.
The census asks people a voluntary question, "What is your religion?".
It can tell us important things about religion but we must interpet it carefully and ask questions about it as a source.
There are reasons why people may not answer or answer the question in a particular way.
Censuses have been used for thousands of years to find out population data, including around the time of Jesus.
keywords: an official count of a country’s population, usually including details like age, sex, and occupation
done by choice, without being forced
involving or including people who follow different religions
a person's connection or association with a specific religion
tips: Take a look at your school's local area religion data using the Office for National Statistics website.

525494791.name: Exploring Christians - diveristy and complexity
525494791.outcome: I can explain why there is diversity within Christianity and give examples of how this is shown.
points: The 2021 census does not give a clear indication of diversity within Christianity but other sources can.
Diversity in Christianity comes from differences in beliefs and practice.
Diversity in Christianity comes from varying interpretations of sources of authority.
The diversity in Christianity is complex and we can use social science data to explore this.
keywords: something or someone that people look to for guidance, rules, or truth
when there are differences between things e.g. in beliefs or practices
tips: Students can explore different denominations in more detail- what are the discinctive beliefs and practices for that denomination and where does this stem from?

844346842.name: Linda Woodhead's exploration of the 'nones' - atheism
844346842.outcome: I can explain what nones are and why this group has increased, using Linda Woodhead's research.
points: People with no religion are known by different terms including 'nones' but nones are not all atheist.
Linda Woodhead is a Professor of Religion and has completed research on the rise of atheism in the UK.
Research suggests the rise is due to factors including upbringing, freedom of belief and the diversity of society.
Woodhead suggets that nones are the 'new norm' which has contributed to its rise.
keywords: a belief that there is no God or higher power/ a lack of belief in ‘God’
people who self-report that they do not affiliate with any religious group
academic who studies the place of religion in modern British society
tips: Students could research and mindmap some of the reasons why people may become athiest.

542816282.name: Linda Woodhead's exploration of the 'nones' - agnosticism
542816282.outcome: I can explain why some of the ‘nones’ may be agnostics and use survey data to better understand this.
points: Agnosticism means believing we cannot know if there is a God or not.
A person may be religious and agnostic.
Using surveys can be a useful way to find out what people believe.
The Understanding Unbelief Project surveyed agnostics and athiests across various countries in the world.
keywords: the belief that it is unknown or unknowable whether any deities exist
individuals who identify as having 'no religion', a term explored in-depth by Linda Woodhead
a global study used to assess agnosticism and related beliefs through survey data
tips: Students can list reasons why people may believe that God exists and reasons why God may not exist and consider how this could influence an agnostic's belief position.

344468282.name: Exploring 'other' religion - Paganism
344468282.outcome: I can explain what Paganism is and give reasons for the growth in numbers in the census of England and Wales.
points: Various different worldviews fall under the term 'Paganism'.
Shamanism is the fastest growing religious group in England and Wales, according to the census.
There are different groups within Paganism, including Wicca and Druid.
Pagan traditions have a focus on the natural world and feminine divine energies.
keywords: an official count of a country’s population, usually including details like age, sex, and occupation
nature is sacred and central to beliefs and rituals
umbrella term for different worldviews often connected to nature, ancient traditions and forms of polythesim
a spiritual practice found in many cultures where a shaman (a healer or spiritual guide) connects with the spirit world to help people
tips: Students can look at a calendar of yearly religious festivals and plot them according to the Pagan Wheel of the Year to see how many of them also fall in certain times, e.g, the Winter Solstice and Christmas.

781828319.name: The future of religion
781828319.outcome: I can explain what the Secularisation Thesis is and how this relates to religion and Generation Z today.
points: The census and other data can show that religion is on the decline in some societies.
The census and other data can show that some forms of religion are not declining in societies.
The Secularisation Thesis states that as societies modernise, religion will be less important and influential.
There is some evidence that Generation Z may be more open to religion than previous generations.
keywords: a group of people born and living around the same time, usually about 20-30 years apart
the idea put forward in social science that as a society becomes more modern it becomes less religious
a sense of connection to something greater than oneself such as a higher power, or nature
tips: Students can explore the census religion data for their local area to see if this follows the national trends as well as explore 'other' forms of spirituality which may appeal to Generation Z rather than organised religion in their area.

582678844.name: Stewardship versus dominion
582678844.outcome: I can explain how Judeo-Christian beliefs about stewardship and dominion influence some human attitudes toward the environment.
points: Philosophy helps us explore big questions about how we treat the world, using reason and logical thinking.
Dominion is a belief that humans were given power by God to rule over the Earth.
Stewardship teaches that humans have a responsibility to care for the world God created and protect it.
Mary Midgley argued that anthropocentrism contributes to environmental destruction.
Instead, she believed humans should see themselves as part of nature, not above it.
keywords: looking after the world on behalf of God
having God-given power or control over the Earth’s resources
seeing humans as central and the most important part of the universe
beliefs shared by Judaism and Christianity
tips: You might like to give students copies of the Biblical passages so they can annotate them and look for evidence. Use 'I do, we do, you do' approaches to aid interpretation. Speak to the Biblical context of these being ancient passages and not written as scientific accounts.

20486262.name: Khalifah: Muslim perspectives on the Earth
20486262.outcome: I can investigate Muslim attitudes to the Earth and explain how some Muslims live out being a khalifah.
points: Within Islam, there is a vision for how to care for the Earth.
The Qur'an speaks of humans are khalifahs who protect the Earth.
The Qur’an emphasises Tawhid and mizan in the khalifah’s role, highlighting the duty to prevent fasad.
Cambridge Central Mosque and Easton Jamia Mosque support Muslims in living out this vision in real, practical ways.
keywords: human stewardship and responsbility for the Earth
corruption and disruption of God’s natural order
tips: Cambridge Central Mosque and Easton Jamia Mosque have excellent resources to supplement this lesson or for further research. A Muslims' guide to climate change is freely available. Students could look at the examples from the hadith and Qur'an to analyse what practical action is suggested and why.

826062973.name: Tikkun Olam and the role of personal responsibility
826062973.outcome: I can explain the Jewish principle of Tikkun Olam and how it encourages personal responsibility to help fix the world.
points: Tikkun Olam is a Jewish concept about 'repairing the world'.
Tikkun Olam has become synonymous with social action and the pursuit of social justice.
World Jewish Relief is an international Jewish humanitarian charity.
The principle of Tikkun Olam influences the work of Jewish charities such as World Jewish Relief.
keywords: the Jewish value of fixing or repairing the world
doing your part to make the world better
the duty to care for God’s world; being a responsible carer
tips: As well as the case study of World Jewish relief, you might like to look at the Eco Judaism movement which is also actively working to help the environment and speak out for the climate. Local synagogues may be involved with this.

328912422.name: Pope Francis and the Laudato Si' encyclical
328912422.outcome: I can explain the message of Laudato Si’ and how it calls people to care for our common home responsibly.
points: Laudato Si' is the name of Pope Francis' encyclical on caring for the planet.
An encyclical is a public letter from the Pope developing Catholic teaching on a topic often in light of current events.
The encyclical begins by quoting St Frances of Assisi, who is the parton saint of animals.
It includes seven key areas of focus which cover poverty, the environment, education and spirituality.
keywords: the Earth we share and must look after
changing how we live to care better for the Earth
treating people, the planet, and relationships as disposable
tips: The Cafod website has some beautiful animations of the encyclical that could be shown. The Laudato Si' centre in Manchester has more detail about their work.

280015234.name: Peter Singer and animal rights
280015234.outcome: I can explain Peter Singer’s argument against speciesism and think about how it can be used to argue for animal rights.
points: Philosophical tools like thought experiments can help us reflect on our own views about animals.
Peter Singer argued against speciesism; the idea it is unfair to treat beings worse just because they are not human.
What matters morally is sentience; the ability to feel pain and pleasure.
Key examples where speciesism often happens are using animals for food and for experiments.
keywords: the belief that one species is more important than another
the ability to experience pain and pleasure
tips: You might like to cut the thought experiment up and allow students to argue for one case and the other. Similarly with the final task they could debate both sides of arguments for the issues raised.

383352689.name: Mary Midgley and why animals matter
383352689.outcome: I can explain Mary Midgley’s argument for why animals matter and explore the issue using philosophical tools.
points: Mary Midgley was a British philosopher known for her work on science, ethics and animal rights.
She said philosophy was useful to help fix our blocked thinking.
She critiques arguments that say animals should be treated exactly like humans and that animals do not matter at all.
'Animals and why they matter' provides philosophical tools we may use to make decisions about the treatment of animals.
She advocates for a mixed community, where animals matter morally for many different reasons.
keywords: our ideas or thinking can sometimes get broken or blocked
animals do not matter morally at all
animals should be treated exactly like humans
belief that humans and animals are fundamentally different groups
tips: Midgley does not give us a checklist for how to treat animals or provide simple answers to every ethical question. Instead, she offers a framework for thinking — philosophical tools that help us reflect more deeply and clearly about our relationships with animals.

480804337.name: Eve and original sin
480804337.outcome: I can retell the Genesis story of Eve and The Fall, and explain different Christian perspectives on this.
points: The Genesis account of Eve and The Fall can be read in different ways, depending on the view of its genre.
Original Sin is a belief that humans are born inclined to sin as a consequence of The Fall.
The story can be read through different lenses which may influence the interpretation of the story.
The story of Eve and The Fall has had different impacts on the view of women within Christianity and wider societies.
keywords: taking something exactly as it is stated without intepreting a deeper or symbolic meaning
the idea that all humans are born with a tendency to sin because of Adam and Eve's disobedience in the Garden of Eden
wrong actions, thoughts or behaviours which go against God's laws and commands
something that represents or stands for a deeper meaning or idea
the event told in Genesis when Adam and Eve disobeyed God, leading to sin entering the world
tips: Showing clips of toddlers refusing to share, siblings pushing one another over and contrasting with toddlers being kind and gentle can stimulate interesting discussions around human nature; are we born with a tendency to sin or to do good?

349660009.name: The song of Deborah
349660009.outcome: I can explain the story of Deborah the judge and prophetess and explain different Christian perspectives on the impact of this.
points: Deborah was an important judge and prophetess in ancient Israel who lead her people to a military victory.
The story of Deborah can impact how women are viewed within religions.
The story of Deborah can inform debates around female leadership and roles within religion.
There can be different perspectives on the impact of the story of Deborah due to the lens through which it is viewed.
keywords: a view that men and women are equal in the eyes of God but have distinct, complementary roles in church and family
a belief in the equality of men and women in all roles, including leadership in the church and family, with no gender-based restrictions
a leader in ancient Israel raised by God to deliver the people from oppression and guide them spiritually, often with military leadership
a female prophet, someone who speaks on behalf of God, delivering prophecy and guidance, like Deborah in the Old Testament
tips: Deborah is one of five prophetesses mentioned in the Old Testament of the Bible. Other prophetesses can be studied as case studies: Miriam, Huldah, Noadia and Isaiah’s wife.

855774168.name: The Book of Esther
855774168.outcome: I can explain the importance of the Book of Esther and how she can be seen as both a victim and a victor in her story.
points: The Book of Esther was written at a time when many Jews were living in exile as a disapora in the Persian Empire.
Esther can be seen as both a victim and a victor in her story.
Esther heard of a plot to kill all Jewish people in Persia and intervened to prevent this happening.
Considering the intended audience of the Book of Esther can help us better understand the significance of the story.

561071748.name: Mary, mother of Jesus
561071748.outcome: I can explain the importance of Mary, the mother of Jesus, across different denominations, and give different perspectives on her ability to be seen as a role model in feminism.
points: Most Christians believe that Mary, the mother of Jesus, was a virgin at the time of his birth, as told in two Gospels.
Across different Christian denominations, Mary is held in high regard for her role in the life of Jesus.
There are different perspectives on whether Mary is a role model for modern-day feminism.
Translations of the original language of a text can influence what meaning is taken from it.

the idea that women should be equal to men

560602893.name: Women in the New Testament
560602893.outcome: I can explain the importance of women in the leadership of the early Church and give different perspectives on this using the writings of Paul.
points: Women have a significant importance in the New Testament writings.
Women were present at both the Resurrection and at Pentecost.
Paul's letters are used to support a variety of views around women's leadership in the Church today.
Junia was a female leader that Paul wrote to, but her name was changed to a male one in later translations of the Bible.
keywords: early Christian leaders responsible for spreading the message of Jesus
the Christian community in the first few centuries after the life of Jesus Christ
a woman mentioned by Paul as ‘well known among the apostles’, depending on the translation
an apostle who spread Christianity and authored many of the New Testament letters
the event when the Holy Spirit came to Jesus' followers, marking the Church's birth
tips: Other women commended for their work for the Church in Paul's letters that can be explored in more depth are Lydia, Phoebe, Priscilla and Aquila.

595966001.name: The Gospel of Mary
595966001.outcome: I can explain how the books of the Bible were chosen and how the Gospel of Mary relates to this.
points: When, where and why texts are canonised can help us better understand the type of authority that the text has.
The Gospel of Mary is believed to be from the second century C.E. and is non-canonical.
Mary Magdalene has a significant role as a leader of the other disciples in this writing.
The Gospel of Mary shows us that the early Christians were debating the role of women in the Church.
keywords: writings that are not officially accepted as part of the Bible, and so are non-canonical.
early Christian leaders responsible for spreading the message of Jesus
books or texts which are officially accepted as part of the Bible
meaning ‘good news'; referring to the teachings and revelation of Jesus Christ
a follower of Jesus, known for her role as a key figure in the early Christian community
tips: Teachers could show different gospels to students, both canonical and apocraphal, without stating if they are in the Bible or not. Information such as the author, content & earliest manuscripts could be shared. Students could then hold their own 'council debates' to decide which should be selected.

759183687.name: Coptic Christianity: Desert Fathers and Mothers
759183687.outcome: I can explain the features of the Coptic church and the impact of Desert Fathers and Mothers.
points: The Coptic church in Egypt is one of the most ancient Christian churches. Tradition says it was started by St Mark.
The Desert Fathers and Mothers were people who chose to live a life as hermits and ascetics in the desert.
The life of St Antony was hugely influential on important figures in western Christianity such as St Augustine.
Figures such as Desert Fathers and Mothers help us understand the diversity of Christian worldviews better.
keywords: belonging to part of the Christian church which began in Egypt
a religious practice of withdrawing from the world to pursue spiritual devotion
a religious man living in spiritual discipline and seclusion
someone who lives simply, giving up comforts to focus on growing spiritually
someone who chooses to live away from other people often in a remote place
tips: There is a rich and distinctive tradition of Coptic art. You might want to find different examples to show students as well as exploring the restoration of the monastrey of St Anthony in Egypt.

677712047.name: Mercy Amba Oduyoye and African Women's theology
677712047.outcome: I can explain how Mercy Oduyoye’s worldview influenced her development of African Women’s theology.
points: Oduyoye showed that African identity and Christianity can be blended rather than being in conflict.
She created a space for African women to shape theology and challenge male-dominated religious traditions.
She encouraged and reimagined areas of theology, such as Christology, from an African woman's perspective.
Her influence continues to inspire African women to lead, rethink and engage in theology.
keywords: focuses on empowering women by integrating their experiences into theological discussions
an indigenous belief system and culture primarily in Ghana and Ivory Coast
taking control of a country and exploiting the resources and people
a system of society where men hold most power and make key decisions
tips: For further reading, look at Dr Oluwatomisin Oredein.

159658456.name: Wangari Maathai and the Green Belt Movement
159658456.outcome: I can explain how Wangari Maathai's worldview inspired her environmental activism.
points: Wangari Maathai was a Kenyan environmental activist who became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
Wangari Maathai started the Green Belt Movement to plant trees in Kenya and fight for women's rights.
Wangari Maathai’s worldview blended her indigenous Kikuyu beliefs with Catholic Christianity.
She argued that the land was sacred and was exploited by colonialism and ideas of dominion from the Bible.
She emphasised re-reading the Bible alongside indigenous beliefs to argue against the exploitation of land.
keywords: one of Kenya’s largest ethnic groups or micro-nations
a person who campaigns to bring about political or social change
taking control of a country and exploiting the resources and people
the idea that God gave humans control over nature
the idea that humanity should look after the world God has created
tips: Wangari Maathai was an inspirational speaker. You may wish to find clips of her speaking. Her story 'The Little Hummingbird' is very simple, and in it she discusses how no-one is too small to make a change.

guidance.label: Depiction or discussion of discriminatory behaviour
guidance.description: Discriminatory behaviour or images, whether on the grounds of race, gender, disability, religion or belief or sexual orientation, or otherwise.

780696072.name: Saint Rose of Lima
780696072.outcome: I can explain the importance of Saint Rose of Lima and her influence today.
points: Saint Rose of Lima was born in Peru to a Spanish father and an indigenous mother.
She was known for her beauty, but rejected marriage and led a life of prayer and solitude.
She was canonised as the first saint in the American continent and is known as the patron saint of indigenous peoples.
Colonisation of South America devastated the indigenous population. Saint Rose is hugely popular with Peruvians today.
Her following can be seen in requests at her sacred well and in her influence on a theology directed to the poor.
keywords: existing naturally or having always lived in a place
someone who lives simply, giving up comforts to focus on growing spiritually
blessed; women who lived religious lives without formal vows or entering a convent
the process of declaring a deceased person a saint
taking control of a country and exploiting the resources and people

397538613.name: Delores S. Williams and womanist theology
397538613.outcome: I can explain how Delores S. Williams’ worldview influenced her development of womanist theology.
points: Williams overcame segregation, personal loss, and societal challenges to become a pioneering womanist theologian.
Her book 'Sisters in the Wilderness' shifted the focus of Christian faith to survival, community, and justice.
Her womanist theology empowers Black women, highlighting their resilience and faith.
Williams' womanist retelling of Hagar's story is significant to many African American women.
keywords: the ability to endure hardship and keep moving forward
persevering through systemic oppression, despite the challenges of racism, sexism and discrimination
highlights Black women’s struggles, strength and faith, addressing both race and gender
tips: Focus on Hagar’s perspective by exploring her resilience and faith through her emotional journey. Encourage students to view her not as a victim, but as a woman of strength and agency, shaped by her experiences and her relationship with God.

165084167.name: Candomblé and Brazilian spirituality
165084167.outcome: I can explain the history of Candomblé and understand some of the ways it is practised.
points: Candomblé is an Afro-Brazilian religion, shaped by Indigenous beliefs and Catholic influence.
It developed as spiritual survival during enslavement, blending Orisha worship with Catholic practices.
Despite oppression and legal bans, Candomblé endured through oral tradition, music, and ritual.
Through divination, priestesses seek messages from the Orishas to guide people through life’s challenges and decisions.
The faith honours connection - to nature, ancestors, and the divine.
keywords: a family member from the past who has died, believed to offer guidance and protection
a practice for understanding spiritual guidance and finding one's Orisha
a branch or denomination within Candomblé
a divine ancestor or spirit; intermediaries between humans and the supreme god, Oludumaré
tips: Several videos and images of drumming and the Yemanjá festival are available online to enhance this section of the lesson.
